tips.title: Below is between, above is outside
tips.body: For a curve opening upwards: **below** the axis is **between** the roots, one interval. **Above** is **outside** them, two pieces. Sketching takes five seconds and makes both obvious, which is why the sketch is the method rather than an extra.

tips.title: Larger number on the left means you are wrong
tips.body: $3 < x < 2$ asks for a number above 3 and below 2 at once, which is nothing. If a double inequality comes out with the bigger number first, the answer was really **two pieces** and needs an **or**.

tips.title: One substitution settles both directions
tips.body: Once you have the roots, substitute any value **between** them. If the quadratic comes out negative, the middle is the $< 0$ region and the outside is the $> 0$ one. That single test replaces the whole sketch.

tips.title: A discriminant condition is a quadratic inequality
tips.body: *No real solutions* means $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, which is usually a quadratic inequality in the unknown letter. $x^2 + kx + 9$ gives $k^2 - 36 < 0$, so $-6 < k < 6$. Recognising the shape makes a hard-looking question routine.

steps.title: Why a sketch decides it
steps.body:
This topic is **Higher tier**.

A quadratic inequality like $x^2 - 5x + 6 < 0$ is asking: **for which values of x is the curve below the x axis?**

That is why the method starts with a sketch. You cannot rearrange your way to the answer, because a quadratic changes sign twice, and a single rearrangement cannot express that.

The method is three steps.

1. Make one side **zero**, if it is not already.
2. **Factorise** and find the roots. These are where the curve crosses the axis.
3. **Sketch** the parabola and read off where it is below, or above, the axis.

For $x^2 - 5x + 6$ the roots are $2$ and $3$, and since $a = 1 > 0$ the curve is a valley. Between the roots it dips **below** the axis; outside them it is **above**.

So $x^2 - 5x + 6 < 0$ has the solution $2 < x < 3$: the part **between** the roots.

steps.title: Less than zero: between the roots
steps.body: When a curve opens upwards, the part **below** the axis is the part **between** the roots. That gives a single interval, written as a double inequality.

check.solution: Roots at $2$ and $3$, curve opening upwards, so it is below the axis **between** them: $2 < x < 3$.

steps.title: Greater than zero: two separate pieces
steps.body:
Turn the inequality round and the answer changes shape completely. The part **above** the axis is **outside** the roots, and that is **two** separate pieces, not one.

This is the single most important thing in the topic. $x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0$ has the solution

$$x < 2 \quad \text{or} \quad x > 3$$

It cannot be written as one double inequality. Writing $3 < x < 2$ says x is bigger than 3 and smaller than 2 at the same time, which nothing satisfies — and it is a very common wrong answer.

steps.title: Getting zero on one side first
steps.body:
Most questions do not arrive with a zero. $x^2 + 3 \leqslant 4x$ has to be rearranged before anything else can happen.

Move everything to one side:

$$x^2 - 4x + 3 \leqslant 0$$

Then factorise as usual: $(x - 1)(x - 3) \leqslant 0$, roots at $1$ and $3$, curve opening upwards, so the answer is $1 \leqslant x \leqslant 3$.

**Move everything to the side that keeps $x^2$ positive.** If you end up with $-x^2 + \dots$, multiply through by $-1$ and **reverse the symbol** — or, better, rearrange the other way in the first place so the problem never arises.

Why it matters: with $a$ negative the curve opens **downwards**, so the part below the axis is now **outside** the roots, and every rule you have just learnt runs backwards. Keeping $a$ positive keeps the rules simple.

steps.note: everything on the side where $x^2$ stays positive

steps.text: $a > 0$, so below or on the axis is **between** the roots

steps.note: and a point outside fails, as it should

check.prompt: Solve $x^2 + 3 \leqslant 4x$. Give your answer in the form a ⩽ x ⩽ b.
check.solution: Rearrange to $x^2 - 4x + 3 \leqslant 0$, factorise to $(x-1)(x-3) \leqslant 0$, roots 1 and 3, so $1 \leqslant x \leqslant 3$.

steps.title: Writing the answer
steps.body:
The shape of the answer follows from which side of the axis you want, and each shape has its own notation.

**One interval**, between the roots:

$$2 < x < 3$$ or in set notation $$\{x : 2 < x < 3\}$$

**Two pieces**, outside the roots:

$$x < 2 \ \text{or} \ x > 3$$ or $$\{x : x < 2\} \cup \{x : x > 3\}$$

On a number line, one interval is a single shaded band between two circles. Two pieces are two shaded rays pointing outwards, with a **gap** between them.

The circles follow the same rule as always: **open** for $<$ and $>$, **filled** for $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$.

For $x^2 - x - 12 \leqslant 0$ with roots $-3$ and $4$, the answer is $-3 \leqslant x \leqslant 4$, and the integers in it are $-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ — **8** values.

**Part C.**

Questions 1 and 2 use the same quadratic and have completely different answers. That contrast is the point of the exercise.

steps.title: Going deeper: the traps and the shortcuts
steps.body:
**Trap 1: writing two pieces as one interval.** $x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0$ is $x < 2$ **or** $x > 3$. Writing $3 < x < 2$ is not merely untidy — it describes the empty set, since nothing is both bigger than 3 and smaller than 2. If your answer has the larger number on the left, you have made this mistake.

**Trap 2: forgetting to get zero on one side.** $(x-2)(x-3) < 6$ cannot be solved by setting each bracket against 6. Expand, subtract 6, and factorise again.

**Trap 3: a negative $x^2$ term.** If you reach $-x^2 + 4x - 3 > 0$, multiply by $-1$ and **reverse**: $x^2 - 4x + 3 < 0$. Forgetting the reversal turns the answer inside out.

**A shortcut worth knowing.** Once you have the roots, you only need to test **one** point to fix the whole answer. Take any number between the roots and substitute it.

- If it makes the quadratic **negative**, then *between the roots* is the negative part, so $< 0$ gives the middle and $> 0$ gives the outside.
- If it makes it **positive**, the curve opens downwards, and everything is the other way round.

One substitution replaces the whole sketch, though sketching is still worth doing because it is quick and it makes the answer obvious.

**A question that looks harder than it is.** *For what values of k does $x^2 + kx + 9 = 0$ have no solutions?* The discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ must be negative, so $k^2 - 36 < 0$ — which is itself a quadratic inequality, with roots $\pm 6$. The answer is $-6 < k < 6$. Recognising that a discriminant condition **is** a quadratic inequality is what makes that question routine.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- This topic is **Higher tier**.
- A quadratic inequality asks **where the curve is above or below the x axis**.
- Method: get **zero on one side**, **factorise** to find the roots, then **sketch** and read off.
- For a curve opening **upwards** ($a > 0$):
  - **below** the axis is **between** the roots — one interval;
  - **above** the axis is **outside** the roots — two pieces joined by **or**.
- $2 < x < 3$ for $x^2 - 5x + 6 < 0$; $x < 2$ or $x > 3$ for $> 0$.
- **Two pieces can never be written as one double inequality.** $3 < x < 2$ describes nothing.
- $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$ **include** the roots; $<$ and $>$ exclude them.
- If the $x^2$ term ends up negative, multiply by $-1$ and **reverse** the symbol.
- One substitution between the roots fixes the whole answer.
- Always check by substituting into the **original** inequality, one point inside and one outside.
- A **discriminant** condition such as $b^2 - 4ac < 0$ is itself a quadratic inequality.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in solving a quadratic inequality?
questions.solution: Get **zero on one side**, then factorise to find the roots.

questions.prompt: The roots of a quadratic are 2 and 3, and it opens upwards. Where is the curve below the axis?
questions.solution: A curve opening upwards dips **below** the axis **between** its roots.

questions.prompt: Which symbols include the roots themselves in the solution?
questions.solution: At the roots the quadratic equals **zero**, so $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$ include them and the strict symbols do not.

questions.prompt: Solve $x^2 - 5x + 6 < 0$. Give your answer in the form a < x < b.
questions.solution: Roots 2 and 3, curve opening upwards, below the axis between them: $2 < x < 3$.
Above the axis is **outside** the roots: two pieces, $x < 2$ **or** $x > 3$.

questions.prompt: Solve $x^2 - 7x + 12 < 0$. Give your answer in the form a < x < b.

questions.solution: Subtract $4x$ from both sides to get zero on one side, keeping the $x^2$ term **positive**: $x^2 - 4x + 3 \leqslant 0$.

questions.prompt: How many integer values of x satisfy $x^2 - x - 12 \leqslant 0$?
questions.solution: Roots $-3$ and $4$, so $-3 \leqslant x \leqslant 4$. That is $-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$: **8** integers.

questions.prompt: A quadratic inequality solution is two separate pieces. How are they joined?
questions.solution: Two pieces are joined by **or**, since a value satisfies the inequality by being in **either** piece.

questions.solution: One substitution between the roots tells you whether the middle is positive or negative, which settles both directions at once.

questions.prompt: What is the set notation for the solution of $x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0$?
questions.solution: Two separate pieces are joined by the **union**. The intersection would be the values in both, which is nothing.

questions.prompt: Solve $x^2 - 7x + 12 > 0$, showing your method, and explain why the answer cannot be written as a single double inequality.
questions.solution: Zero is already on one side, so begin by factorising. The quadratic factorises to x minus three, times x minus four, so the roots are three and four. Since the coefficient of x squared is positive, the curve opens upwards, which means it lies above the x axis on the two outer parts and below it between the roots. The inequality asks where the expression is greater than zero, so the solution is the two outer parts: x is less than three, or x is greater than four. This cannot be written as a single double inequality such as four is less than x is less than three, because that would require a number to be greater than four and less than three at the same time, and no number satisfies both conditions. The solution is two separate pieces with a gap between them, so the two parts have to be joined by the word or.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Solving.** Zero is already on one side, so factorise:

$$(x - 3)(x - 4) > 0$$

The roots are **3** and **4**. Since $a = 1 > 0$ the curve opens **upwards**, so it is **above** the axis **outside** the roots.

$$x < 3 \quad \text{or} \quad x > 4$$

**Why it cannot be one interval.** Writing $4 < x < 3$ would require a number **greater than 4 and less than 3 at the same time**, and no number is. The solution is two separate pieces with a gap between them, so they must be joined by **or**.

If your answer ever has the larger number on the left of a double inequality, this is the mistake.

questions.prompt: Find the values of k for which $x^2 + kx + 9 = 0$ has no real solutions.
questions.solution: A quadratic equation has no real solutions when its discriminant is negative, that is when b squared minus four a c is less than zero. Here a is one, b is k and c is nine, so the discriminant is k squared minus thirty six, and the condition is that k squared minus thirty six is less than zero. This is itself a quadratic inequality in k. Factorising as a difference of two squares gives k minus six, times k plus six, less than zero, so the roots are six and minus six. The coefficient of k squared is positive, so the curve opens upwards and lies below the axis between its roots. The solution is therefore that k lies strictly between minus six and six. As a check, taking k equal to zero gives x squared plus nine equals zero, which has no real solutions, as required.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The condition.** No real solutions means the discriminant is **negative**:

$$b^2 - 4ac < 0$$

With $a = 1$, $b = k$, $c = 9$:

$$k^2 - 36 < 0$$

**This is a quadratic inequality in k**, which is the insight that makes the question routine.

**Solving it.** $(k - 6)(k + 6) < 0$, roots $\pm 6$. The curve opens upwards, so below the axis is **between** the roots:

$$-6 < k < 6$$

**Check.** $k = 0$ gives $x^2 + 9 = 0$, which has no real solutions ✓.

examTechnique.body:
Always get **zero on one side** first, and rearrange so the $x^2$ term stays **positive**. That keeps the rules the simple way round.

Factorise to find the roots, then **sketch**. The sketch is quick and it makes the direction obvious, which is where the marks are lost.

Decide the shape of the answer before writing it: below the axis gives one interval, above gives two pieces joined by **or**.

If your double inequality has the larger number on the left, stop — the answer was two pieces.

Use $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$ to include the roots, and the strict symbols to exclude them, matching the inequality you were given.

Check by substituting into the **original** inequality: one value inside your solution and one outside.
examinerErrors: Writing two pieces as a single double inequality, such as 3 < x < 2.
Reading the wrong side of the axis, giving the complement of the right answer.
Forgetting to get zero on one side before factorising.
Multiplying by −1 without reversing the inequality.
Excluding the roots when the symbol is ⩽ or ⩾.
Solving the equation and stopping, giving only the roots as the answer.
Checking against the rearranged inequality rather than the original.
Treating a discriminant condition as an equation rather than an inequality.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer sketches without being told to, because the sketch is what makes the direction obvious, and it states which side of the axis it is reading before writing anything down. It knows the two shapes of answer and chooses between them deliberately, so it never produces a double inequality with the larger number first. It substitutes into the original inequality to check, using one value inside and one outside. And it recognises a discriminant condition as a quadratic inequality in disguise, which turns the hardest question in this topic into the same three steps as the easiest.
